INTEREST OF AMICUS CURIAE1
Amicus curiae is the Civil Rights Clinic (“CRC”) of
Howard University School of Law, the nation’s first
historically Black law school. For more than 150 years
since its founding during Reconstruction, the law
school has worked to train “social engineers,” as civil
rights giant and former Dean—Charles Hamilton
Houston—called them: lawyers devoted to the pursuit
of human rights and racial justice. As part of its
mission, the CRC advocates on behalf of clients and
communities fighting for the recognition of civil rights
guaranteed by the United States Constitution. The
CRC recognizes that we are currently experiencing a
hate-crime crisis in America that is fueled, in part, by
access to AR-15s and similar semiautomatic rifles
that are pervasive among perpetrators of biasmotivated violence. The CRC believes that
eliminating hate crimes requires that federal, state,
and local governments have the latitude to adopt
measures that allow for reasonable regulation of
deadly assault weapons.
The CRC brings a long-standing record of work
around racial violence in America to this brief. This
history warns us that targeted communities suffer
most when their attackers are armed with destructive
weapons.
To facilitate this Court’s consideration of the
question presented, this brief provides what neither
party does: an overview of the modern-day hate-crime
crisis that we face in America, how it is exacerbated

1 Pursuant to Rule 37.6, Amicus certifies that no counsel for

2
by widespread use and proliferation of AR-15s and
similar rifles, and an account of the historical
tradition that denied armed mobs the means to
terrorize the communities they targeted.
INTRODUCTION & SUMMARY OF
ARGUMENT
The Second Amendment inquiry asks whether the
challenged laws are “relevantly similar” to historical
regulation in “how” and “why” they burden the right.
United States v. Rahimi , 602 U.S. 680, 692 (2024);
N.Y. State Rifle & Pistol Ass’n v. Bruen, 597 U.S. 1, 29
(2022). A modern law need not be a “historical twin.”
Bruen, 597 U.S. at 30. “[C]ases implicating
unprecedented societal concerns or dramatic
technological changes may require a more nuanced
approach.” Id. at 27. Indeed, “when the modern law
addresses a situation that could not have arisen when
the Second or Fourteenth Amendment was adopted, it
is too much to demand such a close match.” Wolford v.
Lopez, 609 U.S. 185, 197 (2026).
This brief addresses one such situation: a crisis in
which perpetrators armed with AR-15s or comparable
assault rifles carry out hate-fueled massacres that, for
most of our history, only an armed mob could
accomplish. In Colfax, Louisiana, in 1873, in
Wilmington, North Carolina, in 1898, and in Tulsa,
Oklahoma, in 1921, massacres in Black communities
took an armed mob. In 2022, it took one perpetrator
and an AR-15. Seeking to kill as many Black people
as possible, he researched ZIP codes to find the one
with the largest Black community within driving
distance of his home. He then drove to a Buffalo
supermarket and killed ten Black people. He chose an
AR-15 because, as he put it, “there are very few

3
weapons that are easier to use and more effective at
killing.” Attacks nationwide—from El Paso, Texas, to
Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, to Colorado Springs,
Colorado—followed the same pattern: an AR-15 or
comparable rifle, hate motivation, and a community
targeted because of race, religion, national origin, or
LGBTQ status.
And just as governments answered the armed mob
by regulating arms, legislatures today may regulate
the weapon that puts a mob’s firepower in the hands
of people bent on carrying out mass hate crime
atrocities. Respondents have shown that the AR-15 is
unusually dangerous and that legislatures have long
restricted weapons of that kind. Amicus does not
repeat that showing. Rather, Amicus makes one
further point. For most of our history, targeting a
community and killing many people before anyone
could intervene largely relied on the existence of
armed groups motivated by bias, and governments
regulated those groups. Laws that regulate the AR-15
carry forward that tradition.
We begin with the history of racial terror. From
Colfax to Wilmington to Tulsa, armed white mobs
killed Black Americans on a scale set by the mob’s size
and the firepower it could assemble. In the infamous
Tulsa massacre, for instance, members of the mob
demanded rifles at the National Guard armory and
looted pawnshops and hardware stores for guns before
they killed as many as they could, destroying a
thriving Black community.
We then turn to how governments responded.
Reconstruction governments disbanded unauthorized
armed organizations and barred firearms from the
polling places, courts, and churches where freed
people were attacked. Those laws addressed a specific
danger: armed groups that could kill or seriously

4
injure many members of a targeted community in a
short time.
Next, we show how the AR-15 has changed that
equation. Most of the deadliest bias-motivated
shootings of the past decade were carried out with an
AR-15 or comparable rifle, selected specifically
because the perpetrators sought to maximize the
death toll. In short, when bias-motivated attackers
have set out to kill as many people as possible, they
have generally chosen this weapon, inflicted mass
casualties, and devastated entire communities in
ways that tear at the fabric of society.
Finally, we explain why that history matters.
Attackers carrying an armed mob’s firepower are an
“unprecedented societal concern[]” that requires
regulation. Bruen, 597 U.S. at 27; see Wolford , 609
U.S. at 197. And laws that regulate AR-15s address
the same danger as the laws that regulated the armed
mob. They are therefore consistent with “the
principles that underpin our regulatory tradition.”
Rahimi, 602 U.S. at 692.
The judgments below should be affirmed.
ARGUMENT
I. Guns Have Long Served as a Racialized
Tool, with Hate-Fueled Violence
Historically Relying on Armed Mobs.
From the Nation’s founding, the right to be armed
functioned as a form of racialized suppression. The
eighteenth-century origins of the right to bear arms
excluded Black people. See Dred Scott v. Sandford, 60
U.S. (19 How.) 393, 417 (1857) (enslaved party),
superseded by constitutional amendment , U.S. Const.
amend. XIV. State law forbade enslaved Black people
from “carry[ing] or mak[ing] use of fire-arms” without

5
written permission from their white enslavers. See,
e.g., An Act for the Better Ordering and Governing of
Negroes and Other Slaves in this Province §§ 25–27
(S.C. 1740), reprinted in  2 Joseph Brevard, An
Alphabetical Digest of the Public Statute Law of
South-Carolina 234–35 (Charleston, John Hoff 1814),
https://shorturl.at/lF4NO. As the country approached
the Civil War, the prospect that citizen rights for
Black people would “give to persons of the negro race”
the right to “keep and carry arms wherever they went”
was proffered for denying those rights. Dred Scott, 60
U.S. at 417.
After slavery was abolished, state laws prohibited
freedmen from bearing arms without a license,
continuing a practice that once authorized white
patrols to raid the homes of African Americans and
confiscate their weapons. Robert J. Cottrol &
Raymond T. Diamond, The Second Amendment:
Toward an Afro-Americanist Reconsideration, 80 Geo.
L.J. 309, 337, 344 (1991), https://shorturl.at/46M6I.
Armed white mobs became especially deadly
during Reconstruction and after. Mob violence
repeatedly terrorized Black communities, with the
size of the slaughter turning on the firepower the mob
could bring to bear. See Franita Tolson, Parchment
Rights, 135 Harv. L. Rev. F. 525, 531 (2022);  see also
McDonald v. City of Chi., 561 U.S. 742, 770–72 (2010)
(plurality opinion) (describing efforts after the Civil
War to keep Black people in the South disarmed and
vulnerable).
On Easter Sunday in 1873, for instance, an armed
white mob attacked dozens of Black residents in
Colfax, Louisiana, in what this Court has called “the
infamous Colfax Massacre.” McDonald, 561 U.S. at
757. Historians estimate that anywhere from 60 to
150 African Americans were killed in one of the

6
bloodiest days of Reconstruction. Danny Lewis, The
1873 Colfax Massacre Set Back the Reconstruction
Era, Smithsonian Mag. (Apr. 13, 2023),
https://shorturl.at/gcFvQ.
A quarter century later, in November 1898, a
white mob wielding rifles and a weapon mounted to a
horse-drawn wagon overthrew the lawfully elected
biracial government of Wilmington, North Carolina.
1898 Wilmington Race Riot Commission, Final Report
(May 31, 2006) [hereinafter 1898 Wilmington Race
Riot Report]; David Zucchino, Wilmington’s Lie: The
Murderous Coup of 1898 and the Rise of White
Supremacy (2021). The mob killed as many as sixty
people, burned the city’s Black newspaper, and drove
the mass exodus of over 2,000 residents. 1898
Wilmington Race Riot Report at 5.
One of the worst acts of racial mob violence in
American history occurred another quarter century
later, on May 31, 1921. That afternoon, the Tulsa
Tribune published a story about a Black teenager
arrested for allegedly assaulting a young white
woman in an elevator. See U.S. Dep’t of Just., C.R.
Div., Review and Evaluation: Tulsa Race Massacre
13–14 (2025), https://shorturl.at/wt8RP. The Tribune
described an unsubstantiated account of a vicious
attack, and rumors of rape spread among white
Tulsans. Id. at 14–16.
Armed Black men, many of them war veterans,
went to the Tulsa County Courthouse to help protect
the Black teenager from an impending lynch mob. Id.
at 17. But the white mob was unexpected in its size
and scope: By late evening, it had swelled to
approximately two thousand people, and its target
was far more than just the accused teenager. Id.
Even worse, the mob was remarkably determined
to arm itself. Hundreds converged on the National

7
Guard armory later that evening, demanding rifles
and ammunition. Id. at 18. The officer on duty turned
them away, but they were undeterred. Id. at 18–19.
Within hours, local police officers deputized hundreds
of white men, and many others looted guns from
pawnshops and hardware stores. Id. at 2, 21–22.
By dawn, as many as ten thousand white Tulsans
massed at the edges of Greenwood, the city’s thriving
Black district. Id. at 26. The mob moved in, and the
once-prosperous community soon became
unrecognizable. Id. As many as three hundred people
were killed. Id. at 51. The mob also reduced thirty-five
city blocks to ashes, including more than one
thousand homes, twenty-four grocery stores, a library,
and about twelve churches. Id. at 2, 27.
Far from isolated episodes, armed mob violence—
often led by white militias—was a recurring form of
racialized oppression during and after
Reconstruction. See Cameron McWhirter, Red
Summer: The Summer of 1919 and the Awakening of
Black America  (2011) (discussing massacres in
Memphis and New Orleans in 1866, East St. Louis in
1917, dozens of assaults during the 1919 “Red
Summer,” and the destruction of Black communities
at Ocoee in 1920 and Rosewood in 1923).
The attacks showed that guns used at scale could
terrorize entire communities along racial lines,
resulting in the loss of life and property as well as
sending chilling warnings to African Americans
across the country that they were unwelcome and
unsafe.

8
II. Reconstruction Governments Regulated
Arms to Protect Black Communities from
Mass Armed Terror.
Modern assault-weapons bans fall within the
regulatory tradition established by Reconstruction
legislatures, which restricted arms to protect Black
communities from terror. Bruen, 597 U.S. at 29
(discussing whether laws are “relevantly similar” to
historical regulations).
In response to the relentless acts of racial violence
by groups that functioned as paramilitaries, the
federal government took action. In 1867, Congress
passed a federal militia law that outlawed any
military organization in the South not a part of the
regular Army. Carole Emberton, The Limits of
Incorporation: Violence, Gun Rights and Gun
Regulation in the Reconstruction South, 17 Stan. L. &
Pol’y Rev. 615, 620–21 (2006). The Army prohibited
the sale of pistols and knives in Charleston, South
Carolina, after several incidents of racialized violence.
Id. at 621. In St. James Parish, Louisiana, all men and
women were prohibited from carrying “guns, pistols,
or other weapons of War.” Id. Eventually, the
Department of the South issued a regional order
outlawing any “[o]rganizations of white or colored
persons bearing arms, or intended to be armed, not
belonging to the military or naval forces of the United
States.” Id.
The Army was not alone in its efforts to stop the
racialized violence it believed stemmed, in part, from
an excess of military weapons in public hands. Some
states amended their constitutions to grant legislative
authority to impose limits and restrictions on carrying
firearms. Id. at 620–21 (documenting how, as “gun
violence against freedmen” became “a dire problem,”
Reconstruction legislatures restricted the carrying of

9
firearms to protect Black citizens); see, e.g., Ga. Const.
of 1877, art. I, § 1, ¶ 22; Tenn. Const. of 1870, art. I,
§ 26; Wyo. Comp. Laws ch. 52, § 1 (1876)
(criminalizing carrying “any firearm or other deadly
weapon, within the limits of any city, town or village”).
Other restrictions sought to disaggregate mob
violence by protecting places where Black citizens
were often targeted. Emberton, supra p.8,  at 615,
620–21. For instance, consider Louisiana’s
restrictions after a massacre in Opelousas, Louisiana.
In September of 1868, armed white mobs in Opelousas
killed about 200 Black people to crush Black political
participation ahead of that November’s presidential
election. Lorraine Boissoneault, The Deadliest
Massacre in Reconstruction-Era Louisiana Happened
150 Years Ago , Smithsonian Mag. (Sep. 28, 2018),
https://shorturl.at/tXouO (recounting the lead-up to
the massacre).  Two years later, Louisiana made it a
crime “to carry any gun [or] pistol . . . on any day of
election” within one-half mile of a polling or
registration place. An Act to Regulate the Conduct
and to Maintain the Freedom of Party Election, § 73,
1870 La. Acts 159, 159–60, available at Duke Ctr. for
Firearms L., Repository of Hist. Gun L.,
https://shorturl.at/F9wm9. And after armed white
men opened fire on a Black political rally, Georgia
prohibited carrying a pistol or other deadly weapon to
any court of justice, or any election precinct, or any
place of public worship. Michael Menkus, Disarm the
Negroes: The Racist Roots of Georgia’s Gun Laws ,
SSRN (Nov. 1, 2007), https://shorturl.at/9nxJv; An Act
to Preserve the Peace and Harmony of the People of
This State, § 1, 1870 Ga. Laws 421, available at Duke
Ctr. for Firearms L., Repository of Hist. Gun L.,
https://shorturl.at/mfgt0.

10
Today, hate-motivated violence persists, and its
perpetrators wield far deadlier weapons than
Reconstruction-era legislatures confronted. With the
AR-15, a single person can command the firepower of
a mob. Bans on assault weapons honor this Nation’s
long and complex tradition of regulating arms to
protect targeted communities from terror and
intimidation. Rahimi, 602 U.S. at 692 (asking
whether a modern law “is consistent with the
principles that underpin our regulatory tradition”). As
these laws demonstrate, the Constitution did not stop
states from preventing armed men from terrorizing
communities because of who their members are.
Presser v. Illinois , 116 U.S. 252, 267 (1886); see also
Bruen, 597 U.S. at 30 (“[It is] settled that these
locations were ‘sensitive places’ where arms carrying
could be prohibited consistent with the Second
Amendment.”).
III. The AR-15 Places the Firepower of the
Mob into the Hands of Hate-Fueled
Perpetrators.
Hate-motivated violence has not ended. Today’s
bias-motivated mass shootings carry forward the
work of the armed mob, but with one big difference:
perpetrators armed with an AR-15 or a similar
semiautomatic rifle can now kill, in minutes, on a
scale that once took many hands. See Br. for Cook

The AR-15 serves that aim. The features that
make it an effective military rifle—the “ability to

deadly than other firearms when used in a mass

The record of bias-motivated attacks bears this
out. Most of the deadliest bias-motivated shootings of
the past decade have involved an AR-15 or
comparable rifle. And several of the attackers have
said in their own words that they chose the weapon to
kill as many people in the targeted community as
possible.

IV. Bias-Motivated Mass Killings Present an
Unprecedented Societal Concern Similar
to That of the Armed Mobs Earlier
Generations Regulated.
The Second Amendment inquiry asks whether a
modern law is “relevantly similar” to its historical
precursors in “how” and “why” it burdens the right.
Rahimi, 602 U.S. at 692; Bruen, 597 U.S. at 29. That
said, a modern law need not be a “historical twin.”
Bruen, 597 U.S. at 30. This Court reaffirmed that
point last Term: “Particularly when the modern law
addresses a situation that could not have arisen when
the Second or Fourteenth Amendment was adopted, it
is too much to demand such a close match.” Wolford,
609 U.S. at 197. And “cases implicating
unprecedented societal concerns or dramatic
technological changes may require a more nuanced
approach.” Bruen, 597 U.S. at 27.
Bias-motivated mass killing by perpetrators
armed with an AR-15 is that kind of situation. Biasbased mass killing was historically a group activity,
because most firearms deployed one shot at a time and
had to be reloaded after every shot. Conn. Br. at 19;
Cook Cnty. Br. at 39. The law addressed the danger of
mass violence by addressing the armed group. Cook
Cnty. Br. at 20 (discussing Pennsylvania and
Massachusetts); Conn. Br. at 36 (discussing armed
groups). The concern behind these laws was that
armed groups “had the capacity to kill or seriously
injure far more people in a short time than a single

recovered an AR-15 rifle and high-capacity magazines, stored
alongside a printed copy of the group’s attack manual and a
notebook listing white supremacist attackers with whom she
corresponded. Gov’t’s Mot. for Det. at 3, United States v. Humber,
No. 2:24-cr-00257 (E.D. Cal. Sep. 10, 2024), Dkt. No. 11.

24
individual ever could before being restrained.” Cook
Cnty. Br. at 20.
Reconstruction governments carried the same
concern forward to prevent armed mobs from
terrorizing Black communities. They disbanded
unauthorized armed organizations and kept arms out
of the polling places and courthouses where freed
people were attacked. See supra Part II.
The AR-15, however, places the firepower of the
mob into the hands of hate-fueled perpetrators, and
the attackers described in Part III chose the weapon
for that reason. See supra  Part III. This new
circumstance deserves close consideration, especially
given the reverberating harms and terrorizing effects
inflicted on immediate victims and entire
communities, not just locally but nationwide. And just
as they have before, legislatures may choose to keep
the mob’s firepower out of the hands of those bent on
committing hate crimes consistent with the Second
Amendment.

to affirm the judgments of the U.S. Courts of Appeals
